clue.text: To wit, unusually nice sort of railway

parts.note: SC is short for scilicet, Latin for 'namely' or 'to wit'

indicators.note: unusually says the four letters of the clue word nice appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Someone describes a pleasant kind of railway, oddly, with a lawyerly 'to wit'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' rearranges NICE into ENIC, placed after SC. A scenic railway is a fairground ride through painted scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground ride of tracks through painted landscapes is known as a scenic railway, so the word names that sort.

clue.text: Seen in many a ship

parts.note: read plainly as a remark about something visible aboard vessels, it describes the goods a freighter carries in its hold

explanation.surface: A remark about what can be spotted aboard ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Freight or goods carried in a vessel's hold are found in most merchant ships.

clue.text: Henry thus called to a raving lunatic

indicators.note: lunatic, meaning crazed, says the letters of the words before it are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone shouts Henry's name at a madman who is ranting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lunatic' scrambles TOARAVING into the epithet of Prince Henry of Portugal, the fifteenth-century patron of voyages of exploration.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Henry of Portugal, who sponsored voyages of discovery, is known by this epithet.

clue.text: Land girl is able to take the lead

indicators.note: to take the lead says the piece for 'is able' goes in front of the girl's name

parts.note: can means is able
Ada is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A Land Girl, one of Britain's wartime farm workers, is capable of leading.
explanation.walkthrough: Land Girls were women who worked on British farms in the World Wars; here 'Land' is the definition, a country.
explanation.definitionFit: The North American nation is a country, and a country is a land.

clue.text: Avoid speed — bad for a bee?

parts.note: to miss something is to avoid it
to pelt along is to go at speed

explanation.surface: Advice to dodge speeding, with a puzzling aside about bees.
explanation.walkthrough: The bee is a spelling bee, a competition where a wrongly written word is fatal.
explanation.definitionFit: A word written with wrong letters would cost a contestant in a spelling competition.

clue.text: Earned easily by oakum-pickers

parts.note: oakum was made by picking apart old tarred ropes, so the idiom for easy gain is read literally as the pickers' wages

explanation.surface: A remark about the pay of prisoners who picked apart rope for oakum.
explanation.walkthrough: Oakum-picking, unpicking old rope into fibre for caulking ships, was a task in Victorian prisons and workhouses.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means payment gained for little effort, and oakum came from unpicked used rope.

clue.text: Cook mince-pies and take one out as a sample

indicators.note: to cook is to doctor or falsify, so the letters of mince-pies are rearranged, less one letter that is taken out

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A kitchen instruction: bake mince pies and remove one to taste-test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' rearranges MINCEPIES, and 'take one out' removes one I (Roman numeral one) from those nine letters, leaving eight.
explanation.definitionFit: A specimen is an example taken to show what the whole is like, the same as a sample.

clue.text: Impervious to piano accompanying musical fiddler?

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
the musical Fiddler on the Roof puts its fiddler on top of a house, so he suggests the top of a building

explanation.surface: A soft piano part goes along with the violinist in a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accompanying' places P alongside ROOF, where the fiddler sits in the musical Fiddler on the Roof. 'Impervious to' works as in 'waterproof' or 'proof against'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being proof against something means resisting it entirely, as in waterproof.

clue.text: Procrustean joker?

parts.note: Procrustes of Greek myth stretched his victims' limbs to fit his bed, so a jesting one would literally stretch lower limbs

explanation.surface: A question about a prankster in the style of the cruel mythical innkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: Procrustes, a bandit in Greek myth, racked short guests to fit his bed; a joker who teases someone is said to stretch their limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who teases by fooling people is said to tug their limb, a practical joker.

clue.text: Bound to accept cooker from this source

indicators.note: to accept here means to take in, so one word is placed within the other

parts.note: to prance is to bound or leap about
an oven is a cooker

explanation.surface: Someone is obliged to take a stove from a particular supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'obliged', but it is a leap, PRANCE; 'to accept' puts OVEN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Provenance is the origin or source of something, especially an artwork's history.

clue.text: Riotous gathering held back by military group

indicators.note: held back says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A wild party is halted by soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden letters YGRO, from the join of 'military group', are read backwards because of 'held back'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild, unrestrained party or revel is a riotous gathering.

clue.text: Showing persistence, followed lady outside

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely

indicators.note: outside picks the outer letters, first and last, of the word lady

explanation.surface: Someone tailed a woman out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' looks like 'out of doors', but it takes L and Y, the first and last letters of 'lady'.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting tenaciously and refusing to give up is showing persistence.

clue.text: Coming in during illness, cross

parts.note: in means during, as in 'in the night'
flu is an illness
X is a cross

explanation.surface: Arriving while ill and feeling irritable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like 'irritable', but it is the letter X.
explanation.definitionFit: An influx is an arrival or inflow, a coming in of people or things.

clue.text: Close finish missed by novelist

indicators.note: finish missed by says the last letter of the novelist's name is dropped

parts.note: Nevil Shute was an English novelist, author of A Town Like Alice

explanation.surface: A tight finish that a writer failed to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close finish' reads as a near-tie, but 'Close' is the definition and 'finish missed by' drops the final E of SHUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: To close a door is to make it fast, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Greeting has little point at the end of this month

definitions.text: at the end of this month

parts.note: hallo is a greeting
wee is Scottish for little
N, north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A greeting that is a bit late, arriving as the month closes.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle presumably appeared in October; the festival falls on the 31st, at that month's end.
explanation.definitionFit: The eve of All Saints' Day falls on 31 October, the last day of that month.

clue.text: Outbid, with a club lead in general

indicators.note: in says the letter from club is put inside the word for general

parts.note: overall means general, as in an overall view

indicators.note: lead picks the first letter of the word club

explanation.surface: In bridge, someone bids higher by leading a club, in general terms.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, to overcall is to bid over an opponent's bid; 'lead' takes C from 'club' and 'in' places it in OVERALL.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge, bidding higher than the previous player's bid is to outbid them.

clue.text: About a friend of mine, chiefly

parts.note: c is short for circa, about
a pit is a mine
an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: A remark about someone's pal from the mine, mostly.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces fall as 'friend of mine' read as ALLY coming after PIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital can mean principal or foremost, so the adverb carries the sense of principally.

clue.text: Job ends just before his work starts

definitions.text: Job ends just before his work starts

parts.words: Job ends just before his work starts
parts.note: in the Old Testament the Book of Job is followed immediately by the Book of Psalms, so its end is just before the songwriter's book begins

explanation.surface: Someone's employment finishes right before their new work begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' looks like employment, but it is the biblical book; David, traditionally the writer of the next book, is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: King David, the traditional writer of the sacred songs that follow the Book of Job, is called this.

clue.text: Jumble sale for Conservative picnic could be so described

indicators.note: jumble means mix up, so the following letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Tory jumble sale where the picnic might be outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumble sale' reads as a charity sale, but 'Jumble' rearranges SALE FOR C.
explanation.definitionFit: A meal eaten in the open air is described with this Italian phrase meaning outdoors.

clue.text: Left harbour

definitions.meaning: the left-hand side of a ship as one faces the bow
a town with a harbour where ships dock

explanation.surface: A ship departed from the harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: The left side of a vessel facing forward has this nautical name, and a harbour town is its other sense.

clue.text: At full speed, there's nobody left in

definitions.meaning: in cricket, the whole batting side has been dismissed

explanation.surface: Running flat out, as nobody is left inside.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a side is finished when ten batsmen are dismissed and nobody is left to bat.
explanation.definitionFit: Going flat out means at maximum effort, and a cricket side with every batsman dismissed has nobody left in.

clue.text: Crowd at the Spanish inn

parts.note: a host is a crowd, as in a host of angels
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A crowd gathers at the Spanish tavern.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are places offering travellers lodging, a youth hostel being a simple inn.

clue.text: Chinese societies used to take sugar

definitions.meaning: a small grip for lifting sugar lumps

explanation.surface: Chinese secret societies in the past took their sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used to' reads as 'formerly' but here means 'employed for'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinese secret societies or brotherhoods carry this name, and small grips for lifting lumps share it.

clue.text: Fish without tail perhaps, making it slow

indicators.note: without means outside, so the fish's letters surround the others

parts.note: a dory is a fish, as in John Dory

indicators.note: perhaps says the word tail is one possible arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A fish with no tail is perhaps sluggish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking: DORY goes round ILAT, which 'perhaps' makes from TAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Dilatory means tardy or given to delay, which is slow.

clue.text: Up in value, having gone like hot cakes

definitions.meaning: having swollen up in the oven as cakes do

explanation.surface: Prices have climbed, as goods sold like hot cakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone like hot cakes' suggests selling fast, but it is the way cakes swell in the oven.
explanation.definitionFit: Prices that have gone up have climbed, and baked cakes swell upward as they cook.

clue.text: Runner broke without one

definitions.meaning: a climbing garden vegetable grown for its long pods
the idiom for having no money at all is to lack even this smallest coin-like thing

explanation.surface: An athlete who is penniless without something.
explanation.walkthrough: A runner is a climbing garden legume; to be without one is to be penniless, as in 'not a ___'.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner is a variety of climbing legume, and someone broke has not a single one to their name.

clue.text: One breaking with tradition stands firm in awful act with lions

indicators.note: in says the firm's abbreviation sits inside the scrambled letters
awful says the letters of act and lions are in a dreadful jumble

parts.note: CO, company, is a firm

explanation.surface: A rebel stands firm during a horrific performance with big cats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges ACT and LIONS into INOCLAST, and 'in' puts CO among them after the I. 'stands' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An iconoclast attacks cherished beliefs and customs, defying tradition.

clue.text: Liqueur I put before Roman

annotationWithheld.why: 'Liqueur I put before Roman' (8): ANISETTE looks like I SET (I put) inside ANTE (Latin 'before'), but no clue word signals the containment and 'put' cannot be both SET and the container

clue.text: Endeavouring to be bothersome

explanation.surface: Making an effort to be annoying.
explanation.definitionFit: Attempting something is endeavouring, and a tiresome person is annoying or bothersome.
